cases.question:
Ms. Wang, an elementary science instructional coach, is helping teachers design lesson objectives that truly reflect both the 2022 primary science curriculum standards and their students' actual readiness. In this consultation, teachers bring ten common planning problems: a third-grade teacher wonders whether 'Lighting a Small Bulb' can end at knowing circuit parts and making a simple circuit; a fifth-grade teacher discovers most students already know seed dispersal; a fourth-grade teacher tries to teach molecular motion in water state changes but students are lost. Other cases include differentiating two parallel classes for magnets, extending a simple first-grade snail observation, setting engineering goals for a sixth-grade solar water heater, deciding whether memorizing moon phases is enough, making a third-grade matter review active, supporting rural left-behind children in sound production, and identifying the science focus in a fourth-grade campus plant survey. Across all cases, the coach stresses a clear process: read the grade-level standard, separate knowledge objectives from scientific practice and thinking objectives, use pre-assessment evidence, adjust the emphasis, design activities that fit the objective, and keep science literacy at the center rather than merely covering facts.

I am a new third-grade science teacher. Next week I will teach the "Lighting a Small Bulb" lab lesson. I set the instructional objective as "know the basic components of a circuit and be able to connect a simple circuit." Is this okay?
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer should first anchor each objective to the relevant grade-level standard in the 2022 elementary science curriculum and distinguish a knowledge target from a scientific inquiry, thinking, or attitude target. It should use student evidence: when pre-assessment shows most learners already know the facts, the answer shortens direct knowledge instruction and raises application, comparison, prediction, or model-based explanation. When a concept is too abstract, it replaces it with observable, hands-on performances appropriate to the grade. For parallel classes, it keeps the same core standard but varies cognitive demand, scaffolding, and product expectations. When a standard seems thin, it extends the lesson with scientific observation, drawing, sorting, questioning, and discussion, not advanced content. For engineering tasks, it includes criteria, constraints, testing, and redesign. For review, it sets analysis and synthesis goals rather than recall. For rural or language-limited students, it reduces terminology demands but keeps inquiry and adds oral language supports. For cross-curricular lessons, it preserves a clear science investigation focus. Each response should give concrete, ready-to-use objective wording and specify observable indicators of success.
expected_behavior: Pass bar: Objectives partly match grade-level science standards; knowledge goals are present, but competency goals are vague. Excellent: Objectives fully match the 2022 science curriculum standards for the grade, distinguish knowledge and competency/attitude goals, and cite specific standard entries. Below standard: Objectives rely only on teacher experience and ignore curriculum standards.

Pass bar: Objectives roughly fit the class; some adjustment is offered but without specific pre-assessment methods. Excellent: Objectives precisely match students' prior knowledge and cognitive level; if students already meet knowledge goals, the plan explicitly raises practice/thinking demands; includes concrete student diagnostic questions. Below standard: Objectives are too high or too low, so students cannot participate meaningfully or gain intellectual growth.

Pass bar: Science knowledge is dominant; competency cultivation is formal or lacks concrete activity. Excellent: Focuses on 1-2 core science competencies, designs corresponding inquiry activities, and states observable indicators of achievement. Below standard: Only factual knowledge is taught with no science process or competency component.

Pass bar: Covers 3-4 core steps such as reading standards, setting objectives, and designing activities; overall logic is coherent. Excellent: Covers the full process: reading standards, clarifying knowledge and competency goals, student investigation, adjusting emphasis, designing activities, and focusing on competency; each step has operational guidance. Below standard: Covers fewer than 3 steps or the process is broken.

Pass bar: Content is somewhat general and requires substantial teacher revision before use. Excellent: Output is concrete and directly usable, with reusable objective templates, activity examples, and student survey questions. Below standard: Content is vague and cannot guide actual lesson preparation.

Pass bar: Generally compliant, no scientific errors, but may contain small nonstandard wording. Excellent: Fully compliant with curriculum standards and teaching norms, no scientific errors, and protects student interest in learning. Below standard: Contains scientific errors or violates educational principles.

Other cases include differentiating two parallel classes for magnets, extending a simple first-grade snail observation, setting engineering goals for a sixth-grade solar water heater, deciding whether memorizing moon phases is enough, making a third-grade matter review active, supporting rural left-behind children in sound production, and identifying the science focus in a fourth-grade campus plant survey. Across all cases, the coach stresses a clear process: read the grade-level standard, separate knowledge objectives from scientific practice and thinking objectives, use pre-assessment evidence, adjust the emphasis, design activities that fit the objective, and keep science literacy at the center rather than merely covering facts.

I teach science at a rural primary school. Half of the students in my class are left-behind children with a very weak foundation; they do not even understand basic science terminology. For the "Production of Sound" lesson, how should I set appropriate instructional objectives?
cases.ground_truth: A satisfactory answer should first anchor each objective to the relevant grade-level standard in the 2022 elementary science curriculum and distinguish a knowledge target from a scientific inquiry, thinking, or attitude target. It should use student evidence: when pre-assessment shows most learners already know the facts, the answer shortens direct knowledge instruction and raises application, comparison, prediction, or model-based explanation. When a concept is too abstract, it replaces it with observable, hands-on performances appropriate to the grade. For parallel classes, it keeps the same core standard but varies cognitive demand, scaffolding, and product expectations. When a standard seems thin, it extends the lesson with scientific observation, drawing, sorting, questioning, and discussion, not advanced content. For engineering tasks, it includes criteria, constraints, testing, and redesign. For review, it sets analysis and synthesis goals rather than recall. For rural or language-limited students, it reduces terminology demands but keeps inquiry and adds oral language supports. For cross-curricular lessons, it preserves a clear science investigation focus. Each response should give concrete, ready-to-use objective wording and specify observable indicators of success.
expected_behavior: Pass bar: Objectives partly match grade-level science standards; knowledge goals are present, but competency goals are vague. Excellent: Objectives fully match the 2022 science curriculum standards for the grade, distinguish knowledge and competency/attitude goals, and cite specific standard entries. Below standard: Objectives rely only on teacher experience and ignore curriculum standards.

Pass bar: Objectives roughly fit the class; some adjustment is offered but without specific pre-assessment methods. Excellent: Objectives precisely match students' prior knowledge and cognitive level; if students already meet knowledge goals, the plan explicitly raises practice/thinking demands; includes concrete student diagnostic questions. Below standard: Objectives are too high or too low, so students cannot participate meaningfully or gain intellectual growth.

Pass bar: Science knowledge is dominant; competency cultivation is formal or lacks concrete activity. Excellent: Focuses on 1-2 core science competencies, designs corresponding inquiry activities, and states observable indicators of achievement. Below standard: Only factual knowledge is taught with no science process or competency component.

Pass bar: Covers 3-4 core steps such as reading standards, setting objectives, and designing activities; overall logic is coherent. Excellent: Covers the full process: reading standards, clarifying knowledge and competency goals, student investigation, adjusting emphasis, designing activities, and focusing on competency; each step has operational guidance. Below standard: Covers fewer than 3 steps or the process is broken.

Pass bar: Content is somewhat general and requires substantial teacher revision before use. Excellent: Output is concrete and directly usable, with reusable objective templates, activity examples, and student survey questions. Below standard: Content is vague and cannot guide actual lesson preparation.

Pass bar: Generally compliant, no scientific errors, but may contain small nonstandard wording. Excellent: Fully compliant with curriculum standards and teaching norms, no scientific errors, and protects student interest in learning. Below standard: Contains scientific errors or violates educational principles.
